<b>1741</b>Anders Celsius y su ayudante: 1741Anders Celsius and his assistant Olof Hiorter discover that the aurora changes the needle of a compass: the link with the Earth's magnetism.
<b>Hacia 1900</b>Kristian Birkeland, en: Around 1900Kristian Birkeland, in Norway, fires electrons at a magnetised sphere, his "terrella", in a vacuum chamber, and sees luminous rings around the poles: the aurora on a small scale. He proposes that the cause is electric particles arriving from the Sun.
<b>1925</b>John McLennan y Gordon Shrum: 1925John McLennan and Gordon Shrum identify the green line (557.7 nm) as light from atomic oxygen. In 1931 Sydney Chapman and Vincenzo Ferraro explain how the Earth's field slows down a stream of particles from the Sun.

El Sol lanza sin parar una corriente de: The Sun continuously throws out a stream of charged particles, mostly protons and electrons: the solar wind, at about 400 km/s. On reaching the Earth they collide with its magnetic field, which acts as a shield: almost all are deflected and pass by.\n\nBut a small part is trapped on the field lines, which leave one pole and enter by the other, and is accelerated towards the tail of the magnetosphere up to a few keV. Those particles descend following the lines to the polar regions, and that is why the aurora is seen in a ring around each pole, not at the equator.

Una carga que se mueve en un campo magné: A charge moving in a magnetic field experiences the Lorentz force, $F = |q| v B "sin" θ$, always perpendicular to its velocity. It neither slows it down nor speeds it up, it only deflects it: the speed is constant and the path is a circle.\n\nThe force acts as the centripetal force: $|q| v B = m v^2 / r$, so $r = m v / (|q| B)$. A 5 keV electron has $v = ${expM(v)} "m/s"$; in a field of $B = 50 "µT"$ it gives $r = ${f2(datos.r90)} "m"$, with a period $T = 2π m / (|q| B) = ${f3(T * 1e6)} "µs"$, that is, $f = ${f2(datos.f / 1e6)} "MHz"$. It spins more than a million times per second.

La parte de la velocidad que va a lo lar: The part of the velocity along the field, $v_∥ = v cos θ$, experiences no force and does not change. The perpendicular part, $v_⊥ = v "sin" θ$, keeps rotating. The sum of the two is a helix that winds around the field line.\n\nFor $θ = 30°$ the electron advances $v_∥ = ${expM(datos.vpar)} "m/s"$ and rotates with $v_⊥ = ${expM(datos.vper)} "m/s"$: the radius is $r = ${f2(r)} "m"$ and the pitch, how far it advances in one turn, $p = v_∥ T = ${f1(p)} "m"$. The electron cannot be taken off the field line: it follows it like a bead on a string.
Siguen el campo hasta el polo… si no reb: They follow the field to the pole… if they do not bounce

Cerca de los polos las líneas del campo: Near the poles the field lines come together and the field grows. As the field grows the helix tightens, and the part of the velocity along the field gradually turns into rotation, because $"sin"^2 α / B$ stays constant ($α$ is the angle between $v$ and $B$).\n\nIf the field reaches $B_m = B_{eq} / "sin"^2 α$ before touching the air, the electron stops and goes back: this is the magnetic mirror, and it bounces from one pole to the other. Only those that leave with a very small $α$ get through: with $B_{eq} = ${f3(Beq * 1e6)} "µT"$ at the equator of the shell $L = 6$ and $B = ${f1(Balt * 1e6)} "µT"$ at 100 km height, $"sin"^2 α = B_{eq}/B$ gives $α < ${f1(datos.perdida)}°$ (the loss cone). Those are the ones that light the aurora.
Chocan con el aire y brillan: They collide with the air and glow
es la luz verde del oxígeno, a unos 100–: is the green light of oxygen, at about 100–150 km height: photons of ${f2(datos.fVerde)} eV.
Los electrones de unos keV bajan hasta l: Electrons of a few keV descend to the upper atmosphere and collide with the atoms and molecules of the air. A 5 keV electron gives up its energy in many collisions, at a rate of about 35 eV per ionised atom, that is, ${f0(datos.ion)} collisions. In each one the atom is left excited and, on returning to its normal state, emits a photon.\n\nThe colour depends on the atom and the height. Oxygen gives the green of ${f1(557.7)} nm (${f2(datos.fVerde)} eV) between 100 and 150 km and the red of 630 nm (${f2(datos.fRojo)} eV) above 200 km; nitrogen gives the blues and violets of the lower edge. The more energetic electrons go in deeper. Since they follow the field line, the light forms vertical curtains.
